#5753. Opinion: AI depends on medical records that don’t always tell the full truth about women

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Annemarie G. Hirsch and Jennifer Silva

Hirsch and Silva are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

In September, the Gallup-Pivotal Women’s Health Survey reported that 34% of U.S. women strongly or somewhat agreed that a health care provider minimized or dismissed their symptoms in the past five years. Thirty-three percent reported being misdiagnosed or unable to get a diagnosis, compared with 21% of men reporting these experiences.

Medical records tell a different story. An epidemiologist and a sociologist, we recently released a study where we paired electronic medical records with detailed interviews with 87 women. We talked to these women about their pain and illnesses, work, family, poverty, violence, and encounters with the health care system.

Fifty-three of the women described a trust-breaking encounter with a health system, but only seven of them had medical records that documented mistrust. Thirty-two women reported experiencing a misdiagnosis, but misdiagnosis was only documented for eight of these women. Thirty women reported that they felt that clinicians treated them with disrespect, but this was not documented in the records anywhere.

For more than a decade, Kate lived with debilitating pelvic pain. Her doctors repeatedly attributed her symptoms to obesity. Her medical record reflected these assumptions.

When Kate underwent bariatric surgery and lost a significant amount of weight, her clinical notes became optimistic.

However, her symptoms persisted. Medical records pivoted from linking symptoms from obesity to mental health factors.

“Gastrointestinal malfunctions arising from mental factors.”

The turning point came only after Kate attended an appointment with her new husband. In the clinical notes, the provider documented Kate’s husband’s concerns:

For the first time in 10 years, doctors conducted the exams needed to finally diagnose Kate with endometriosis.

Kate’s medical record accurately documented years of conversations about weight and mental health. What it failed to capture was equally important: the cost of years spent with an undiagnosed disease, the frustration of not being believed, and the erosion of trust that occurs when symptoms are repeatedly explained away rather than investigated. Kate told us, “If I was tired, it was because I was overweight. If I had cramps, it was because I was overweight. Migraines, I was overweight. … They’re not hearing what you’re saying, and that compounded the issues that were going on.”

We often think of medical records as objective accounts of a patient’s health. They are not. Medical records are narratives, shaped by the questions clinicians ask and the assumptions they bring into the room. Medical record data reflect clinical decisions as well as biology. The language clinicians use and the details they choose to record can reinforce stereotypes that follow patients from one encounter to the next, influencing how future clinicians interpret symptoms, assess credibility, and make treatment decisions.

Medical record data also reflect what patients feel comfortable disclosing. What women share with their doctors depends on how much they trust them and how safe they feel. When people fear judgment, dismissal, or not being believed, important parts of their stories may remain unspoken, and thus, undocumented.

This fear may why 53 women in our data described a trust-breaking clinical encounter in their interview, while only seven of their medical records noted their mistrust. This is particularly a problem for women, who feel the pressure to be pleasant and pliant with doctors for fear of not being taken seriously.

Across the country, clinics and hospitals are adopting AI scribes that transcribe recorded interactions between doctor and patient and produce a clinical note. AI tools can be used to search and synthesize medical records to help with diagnostics and treatment plans, some with great success.

However, these tools are only as good as the data in the medical record. If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.

For AI to achieve its full potential in women’s health, medical records need to tell the complete story. Health care settings must be safe spaces where women can tell their stories; clinicians need to listen to women, even when their experiences do not fit clinical expectations; and clinicians need to document in the medical record when diagnoses are delayed or incorrect, without fear of being penalized.

Armed with these data, AI has the potential to do more than replicate biases of the past. AI could help identify patterns of missed diagnoses, reduce disparities in care, and ensure that more women are heard.

Annemarie G. Hirsch, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Jennifer Silva, Ph.D., are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

#5752. The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut

Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between the bacteria living in the human gut and the speed at which the body ages. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that certain gut microbes are associated with slower biological aging, while others are linked to faster aging.

The study, published in Scientific Reports, found that differences in gut bacterial communities accounted for approximately 15% of the variation in participants' biological aging rates. The results suggest that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive system, may provide valuable clues about aging at the molecular level.

"This study advances our understanding of the relationship between the gut microbiome and biological aging," said senior author Alika K. Maunakea of the UH Mānoa John A. Burns School of Medicine. "We found that microbial patterns in the gut were significantly associated with molecular measures of aging, even independent of chronological age. These findings open important new directions for understanding how modifiable biological systems influence long-term health trajectories and longevity."

Scientists Identify Gut Bacteria Linked to Faster and Slower Aging

To investigate the relationship between gut bacteria and aging, researchers examined stool and blood samples collected from 123 adults across a wide range of ages. They identified the bacteria present in each participant's gut and compared those findings with blood-based molecular markers used to estimate the body's rate of aging.

These biological measurements differ from chronological age, which simply reflects how many years someone has been alive. Instead, they are designed to assess how quickly aging-related changes are occurring within the body.

The researchers found a notable association between the composition of the gut microbiome and DunedinPACE, an advanced biomarker that measures the pace of biological aging.

Some bacterial species stood out for their particularly strong relationships with aging. Bifidobacterium adolescentis was among the microbes most strongly associated with slower biological aging. In contrast, Succinivibrio dextrinosolvens showed one of the strongest associations with faster aging.

These differences suggest that particular patterns of gut bacteria may offer important information about how rapidly the body is aging.

How Diet, Lifestyle, and Environment May Influence Gut Health

Lead author Braden P. Kunihiro said the discovery adds to growing evidence that the gut microbiome could play an important role in precision health research, which aims to better understand individual differences in health and disease.

Unlike chronological age, the composition of the gut microbiome can change in response to everyday influences, including diet, lifestyle, and environmental conditions. This makes it a particularly interesting area of investigation for scientists studying healthy aging.

"The gut microbiome is highly responsive to lifestyle, diet, environment and other everyday exposures," Kunihiro said. "Our findings suggest that the microbiome may reflect important aspects of biological resilience and aging in ways that could eventually help inform future wellness and healthy aging strategies."

The research also included Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander participants, groups that have historically received limited representation in studies of aging and gut microorganisms.

Co-author Ruben Juarez explained that including these populations could help scientists investigate how social circumstances and environmental conditions leave lasting biological effects over the course of a person's life.

"The microbiome exists at the intersection of behavior, environment and human biology," Juarez said. "Studies like this help illuminate potential pathways through which lived experiences and social factors influence long-term health outcomes."

Could Changing Gut Bacteria Influence How We Age?

Although the findings reveal a meaningful relationship between gut bacteria and biological aging, researchers stress that the study does not establish cause and effect. In other words, finding certain microbes in people who age more slowly does not necessarily mean those bacteria are responsible for slowing the aging process.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether deliberately changing the gut microbiome can influence biological aging or improve long-term health.

Still, the findings offer a promising starting point for exploring how the microorganisms living inside us relate to the aging process and whether they could eventually help guide more personalized approaches to healthy aging.

"This is an important early step toward understanding the gut microbiome's relationship with healthy aging," Maunakea said. "Future research will help clarify the mechanisms involved and whether these microbial signatures may eventually contribute to precision approaches for promoting long-term health and wellness."

Materials provided by University of Hawaii at Manoa. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5751. STAT+: After Medicare punts RPM overhaul to 2029, advocates see window to fight back

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Mario covers technology in health care, including FDA regulation of artificial intelligence; how Medicare pays for health tech; the use of AI in clinical care; mental health chatbots; and consumer wearables. He’s also the co-author of the free, twice weekly STAT Health Tech newsletter. You can reach Mario on Signal at mariojoze.13.

Medicare regulators this week pushed forward with a controversial plan to ban hospitals and other providers from using third parties to deliver remote patient monitoring services, despite overwhelming opposition from health tech companies, hospitals, insurers, and specialty organizations.

But regulators also offered providers a reprieve in the form of a two-year delay in implementation that’s aimed at allowing time for providers to build in-house services. Advocates representing vendors, hospitals, and other stakeholders see that window as an opportunity to push for another plan.

“The story is that we have two years to come up with something better,” said Christopher Adamec, a lobbyist who advises the Remote Monitoring Leadership Council, a group of leading vendors. “My mission here is to find and move forward a value-based payment pathway or some set of guardrails, or some alternative to this.”

#5750. Avanlee Care, platform for family caregivers, raises $3.5M, targeting Medicare Advantage plans

Avanlee Care, platform for family caregivers, raises $3.5M, targeting Medicare Advantage plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Avanlee Care, a platform to engage family caregivers, has clinched $3.5 million in seed funding, Fierce Healthcare has learned.

The round was led by BEA Venture Fund, with participation from angel investor Esther Dyson, who is Avanlee’s board chair, Chrysalis Ventures and FairBridge VC. Avanlee will use the capital, which brings its total raised to $6 million, to expand across the Medicare Advantage market.

Avanlee Care helps MA plans and other organizations engage caregivers within their member populations, enabling caregivers to take action and organizations to measure the impact. On the Avanlee platform, caregivers can schedule appointments, manage medications, connect with retailers, communicate with their plan and provider, get vaccination reminders and search for providers. Meanwhile, payers get insight into caregiver burnout and member health trend data.

“Avanlee Care is addressing an enormous and underutilized resource within healthcare,” Melissa Bradley, founder and managing partner of BEA Venture Fund, said in a comment. “As healthcare organizations look for more effective ways to improve engagement and outcomes, Avanlee is offering the infrastructure to make caregivers part of that strategy. We believe that creates a significant opportunity to improve both the caregiver experience and healthcare outcomes at scale.”

Founded in 2020, Avanlee began as a direct-to-consumer app, since transitioning into the enterprise space. It is fully integrated with Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drugs as its lead pharmacy partner for discounted medications, and is in discussions with a national, undisclosed MA plan to bring its platform to members with an assigned caregiver. As part of an initial potential pilot with this plan, thousands of members with an assigned caregiver would participate in Avanlee, with a broader expansion planned for mid-2027. Additionally, Avanlee is working toward a separate unnamed integration with a national pharmacy partner for delivering medications.

“We are excited to work with Avanlee Care. We share a common mission: to provide lower costs on prescribed medications, saving money for the unpaid family caregiver and their loved one, the care-receiver,” Mark Cuban, co-founder of Cost Plus Drug Company, told Fierce Healthcare.

Nearly 1 in 4 Americans provide ongoing care for an adult or child with a complex medical condition or a disability, coordinating medications, appointments, transportation, food and other needs. Yet by overlooking the person managing a member’s care and day-to-day living, plans’ efforts to engage MA members are less effective, Avanlee executives argue.

“Caregivers spend an astronomical amount of time having to juggle their career, their families, and suddenly now I’m thrust into this role of I’m a caregiver for my mom … so saving time is huge,” Avanlee Christine, co-founder and CEO of Avanlee Care, told Fierce Healthcare exclusively. Christine, who grew up with a grandfather with Parkinson’s and dementia, was inspired to build the platform that could have supported her mom when she was caregiving.

Avanlee offers caregiver wellness tools on its platform, which 59% of past users have engaged with. Over half of consistent users also reported a decrease in overall stress. In its DTC days, Avanlee supported thousands of families, claiming it saved their caregivers thousands of hours. The wellness tools include a weekly questionnaire on stress and educational resources on topics such as estate planning, life planning and legal services. Caregivers can add other relatives to the platform for extra visibility or support, and Avanlee also facilitates grocery delivery through an integration with Walmart (their pricing applies). “If the caregiver fails, the one ultimately receiving care fails,” Christine said.

This stress survey becomes a key data stream for Avanlee plan partners, allowing them to evaluate caregiver burnout. Avanlee's platform also provides payers with insights about appointment bookings, home health services and medication adherence.

There’s a reason Avanlee is targeting MA to start. Nearly two-thirds of caregivers say MA makes caregiving duties easier to manage than traditional Medicare, according to one survey. Avanlee is also interested in eventually expanding to dual-eligibles. "There's a lot of tailwinds in caregiving for both Medicare and Medicaid and those dually eligible populations,” Eric Scott, Avanlee’s chief growth officer, said.

In order to streamline scheduling, Avanlee is seeking MA partners that allow it to also tap into their provider networks. Avanlee can automatically schedule appointments when prompted by a health plan, such as annual wellness visits or cancer screenings. Caregivers can also manually add their existing appointments to get reminders. In the near future, Avanlee plans to let caregivers book ad hoc appointments for needs beyond those specifically requested by the health plan.

Avanlee charges payers per-member-per-month and is available at no direct cost to the caregiver. It behooves plans to support this population, Christine argues, not only because of their influence over member outcomes but also because they could become a loyal future customer base. “You want to build a relationship with that adult daughter or son because you take such good care of their mom,” Christine said.

Avanlee is incorporating AI to reduce friction for caregivers, like summarizing caregiver notes recorded via audio, recommending providers based on caregiver preferences and matching users’ questions with curated resources. It also makes recommendations to caregivers based on a number of insights, including what medications a member is taking, what conditions they have and what their social needs are. These AI features are powered by AWS Bedrock, with requests handled within Avanlee’s cloud environment rather than being sent to a third-party model provider.

“How do we make it the new norm in healthcare that these people are part of healthcare for mom or dad on day one,” Christine said.

#5749. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

#5745. NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon

NASA's Artemis I mission has provided new insights into how much cosmic radiation astronauts may encounter near the Moon compared with low Earth orbit. Using experimental detectors made from lithium fluoride crystals aboard the Orion spacecraft, researchers have obtained preliminary measurements that reveal unexpected differences in radiation exposure between the two environments.

During the uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022, Orion traveled around the Moon carrying more than 10,000 tiny crystals embedded inside two human-shaped mannequins. These devices recorded radiation exposure throughout the journey. Among them were several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors created by scientists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. The researchers have now described a new method for analyzing the information stored in these crystals, offering insights into both cosmic radiation levels and the performance of the detectors. Their findings were published in the journal Radiation Measurements.

"The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope," explains Prof. Pawel Bilski (IFJ PAN), one of the co-authors of the paper.

How Tiny Crystals Detect Cosmic Radiation

The lithium fluoride detectors work by capturing microscopic changes caused by radiation. When electrically charged particles pass through a crystal, they disrupt its internal atomic structure, creating defects known as color centers. Scientists can later illuminate the crystal with blue light, causing these altered regions to glow red. By examining that fluorescence under a microscope, researchers can identify the paths taken by individual radiation particles.

The detectors were part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study conducted during Artemis I. Several dozen experimental lithium fluoride detectors were placed inside both mannequins, including some containing high concentrations of the lithium-7 isotope. The contribution from IFJ PAN extended beyond these experimental devices. Its scientists also supplied nearly 600 thermoluminescent crystal detectors, which use a different technique to measure radiation exposure.

One major advantage of the new lithium fluoride detectors is that they simplify the process of examining radiation tracks. Traditional passive detectors made from plastic require chemical etching before scientists can study the marks left by incoming particles. Lithium fluoride crystals eliminate that step, allowing researchers to inspect the tracks directly with a standard fluorescence microscope.

As a result, observing the radiation tracks collected near the Moon was relatively straightforward. The more difficult task was determining exactly what those tracks revealed about radiation exposure. To obtain reliable numerical measurements, the team had to develop sophisticated calibration and analysis techniques.

Why Measuring Deep Space Radiation Is So Difficult

Unlike the controlled conditions of a laboratory, cosmic radiation is highly unpredictable. In a typical physics experiment, researchers can expose a detector to a beam containing a known type of particle with a specific energy and direction. In space, radiation arrives from every direction and includes many different particles and atomic nuclei traveling across an enormous range of energies.

This complexity makes the microscopic tracks difficult to interpret. Because incoming particles strike the crystals at different angles, their tracks extend in multiple directions. A microscope captures the section of each track within its focal plane (approximately one micrometer in size), but it also records a blurry glow from portions outside that narrow region. This additional light influences the measured fluorescence intensity, which scientists use to estimate how densely a particle ionizes the material.

Different particles also produce very different track patterns. Those that cause strong ionization leave continuous, sharply defined lines, while particles that produce weaker ionization may appear as scattered, disconnected dots. These differences further complicate the task of translating fluorescence measurements into meaningful radiation data.

To overcome these challenges, the researchers introduced several corrections and developed software capable of removing unwanted background signals. The improved analysis brought their measurements into close agreement with results from established detector technologies while also revealing radiation events that older devices could not detect.

"After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date," Prof. Bilski emphasizes.

Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Difference in Moon Radiation

The Artemis I measurements also allowed researchers to compare radiation exposure near the Moon with findings from an earlier experiment aboard the International Space Station.

More than a decade before Artemis I, the MATROSHKA experiment investigated radiation exposure using human-shaped mannequins on the space station. Some of the radiation recorded during that mission came from low-energy protons trapped within Earth's Van Allen radiation belts. As these particles traveled into the mannequins, they deposited energy at different depths, producing an uneven distribution of radiation doses.

Conditions near the Moon are substantially different. The Van Allen belts do not extend into the lunar environment, so the radiation encountered there contains a greater contribution from high-energy particles originating elsewhere in the galaxy.

These galactic particles carry enough energy to travel through the entire human body, releasing only a portion of their energy as they pass. Consequently, the Artemis I detectors recorded radiation doses that were distributed almost uniformly throughout the mannequins, unlike the uneven patterns observed in the earlier space station experiment.

The researchers also identified a finding that may seem counterintuitive. Although astronauts near the Moon are exposed to more radiation than those in low Earth orbit, the difference is not necessarily as dramatic as might be assumed.

"Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet's magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect," Prof. Bilski notes.

New Radiation Detectors Could Help Protect Future Astronauts

The fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors aboard Artemis I were manufactured using the Czochralski method, a technique for growing crystals. Scientists at IFJ PAN first developed the technology about a decade ago and have continued refining it ever since.

Their compact size is one of their most useful features. Measuring just a few millimeters rather than several centimeters (on the order of millimeters rather than centimeters), the detectors are small enough to be worn comfortably by people, making them practical for monitoring radiation exposure during space missions.

They also provide sharper images of particle tracks than conventional plastic detectors that require chemical etching. This improved resolution allows scientists to distinguish individual tracks even when radiation doses are relatively high. In addition, the crystals can register a broad variety of particle types and energies, potentially providing a more complete picture of the radiation environment.

Another advantage is their ability to detect neutrons, particularly when the crystals are enriched with the lithium-6 isotope. When neutrons interact with lithium nuclei, they can trigger nuclear reactions that generate secondary charged particles. These particles leave detectable changes in the crystal, much like other forms of ionizing radiation.

Together, these capabilities make lithium fluoride detectors a promising tool for studying the complex radiation environment beyond Earth. The measurements from Artemis I offer a clearer picture of how cosmic radiation behaves near the Moon and demonstrate how compact detectors could help scientists evaluate radiation exposure during future missions.

The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

Oh, and a study that unearths evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb (pun intended). Let’s dig in.

That’s how much higher the risk of brain bleeding during the first six months of life was in infants who didn’t receive a vitamin K shot, compared to those who did. Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, which plays an essential role in forming blood clots. That’s why the American Academy of Pediatrics has for more than 60 years recommended that newborns get the one-time shot shortly after birth. But medical mistrust has led a growing number of parents to turn down the injection; the share of newborns who weren’t given vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025.

That trend has had grim consequences, according to a study published Thursday in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Researchers looked back on data from more than 5 million infants born between 2017 and 2025 and found that, compared to infants given vitamin K, those who weren’t given K had a 47% higher risk of bleeding during their first six months and a 169% higher risk of dying while bleeding shortly after birth.

In recent years, the Kratom plant and related synthetic products have become omnipresent across smoke shops and gas station shelves, buoyed by proponents who extol these products’ pain-relieving powers. But public health experts have raised serious concerns about the potential dangers of kratom — and the fact that these products are not closely regulated.

It’s a debate that is confusing to many; two-thirds of Americans have never even heard of kratom. STAT’s Theresa Gaffney has you covered with this timely explainer on the drug. The piece covers how a plant that has been chewed and brewed for centuries in Southeast Asia due to its stimulant-like effects has quickly risen in popularity in the U.S., where some users say kratom has eased chronic pain and helped them get off opioids.

Theresa also digs into 7-OH and MGPI, semi-synthetic related products that some experts worry are especially addictive. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say that they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular. But for now, data on overdoses and deaths are murky.

You might think that your medical records are an objective account of your health. But they’re not, write epidemiologist Annemarie Hirsch and sociologist Jennifer Silva. The pair recently published a study in which they paired electronic medical records and interviews with 87 women about pain, illness, and encounters with the health care system.

Many of the women described trust-breaking encounters with health care providers and misdiagnoses, but these moments were rarely documented. The authors point to the story of a woman who lived with debilitating pelvic pain for more than a decade as a poignant example. Doctors at first dismissed her pain as related to obesity, pivoting to mental health after she lost weight. Notably, the turning point only came after her husband joined her for an appointment, and she was ultimately diagnosed with endometriosis. Her medical records chronicle this diagnostic odyssey, but they don’t capture the frustration and disillusionment she experienced after years of having her pain downplayed. Hirsch and Silva write that such stories raise concerns about the use of AI to advance women’s health.

“These tools are only as good as the data in the medical record,” they write. “If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.”

Many Democrats are still celebrating the blue wave that handed their party control of both the House and Senate. But that momentum didn’t fully translate to health-related ballot initiatives across the country. As of late Thursday, voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington had approved or were on track to endorse measures that would prohibit transgender youth from participating on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Voters in four states with abortion-related ballot measures chose to preserve the status quo, with Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia choosing to maintain abortion rights while Idaho preserved the state’s existing ban.

Meanwhile, California voters appear on track to endorse Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research. The measure has sparked controversy because its main backer is also the co-founder of an institute poised to receive half the funds. South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned a state Medicaid expansion on federal financial support holding steady. And Massachusetts voters can breathe easier (well, sort of) after a measure to repeal the state’s recreational marijuana law was defeated handily.

You can read more from me and Theresa Gaffney. But first, let’s stick with weed for a moment longer.

Early writing by the ancient Greek historian Herodotus — known for his foundational text on the Greco-Persian wars and banger quotes like, “of all possessions a friend is the most precious” — is a key source used by historians to support the idea that prehistoric communities were smoking weed. Archaeological evidence is hard to come by (plants are perishable!) and just as tricky to interpret. But a new paper, published yesterday in Science, offers compelling evidence of ritual cannabis use in a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb.

The monumental burial mound included a log cabin-like structure, one coffin, and the remains of multiple individuals and horse sacrifices. There, archaeologists found hundreds of cannabis seeds, a handful of which were analyzed and dated to the first decade of the eighth century BCE. But there was an even rarer finding: two long braids of human hair containing significant amounts of the psychoactive compound cannabinol. “Although proving intent in a prehistoric context will remain impossible,” the authors wrote, “the evidence is strongly in favor of intentional consumption for the plant’s psychoactive properties.”

Admittedly, this is not our usual fare. But the study is a good reminder that drug use is not a modern issue, but rather a phenomenon that’s been with us for millenia. — Theresa Gaffney

#5743. Study Finds Evidence of Cannabis Use 2,800 Years Ago

— Findings point to consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use

People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought -- at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests.

Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes.

The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China.

Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands.

The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden, and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies.

"It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said study author Gino Caspari, PhD, MSc, an archaeologist at the University of Bern.

It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said.

The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians -- ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine.

The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts, and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe.

Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear, and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said.

"It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said.

Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said.

Results were published in the journal Science.

Not all independent experts were convinced.

The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, PhD, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email.

"For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)."

Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses -- seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth -- their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use.

Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure -- in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange.

But Elisa Guerra Doce, PhD, of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study.

In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite."

#5742. CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes

CMS’ final 2027 outpatient pay rule brings hospitals little relief on 340B, site-neutral changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services on Tuesday finalized its annual outpatient hospital payments rule with a lower-than-proposed rate bump and its major, industry-opposed policy shifts moderated, but largely intact.

The 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) and Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Payment Systems rule outlines a 2.3% reimbursement increase for those meeting applicable quality reporting requirements. That’s below the proposed 2.4% increase and reflects a 3.2% projected hospital market basket increase and a 0.9 percentage point productivity adjustment.

The agency is also moving forward with a substantial and controversial cut in 340B drug reimbursements, though not quite to the extent that it initially proposed.

The final rule adjusts these drug payments down from the current bar of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% to ASP minus 28%, as opposed to the proposed 33.4% below ASP. To make the reimbursement change budget neutral as required by statute, OPPS payments for non-drug services will be boosted by 7.5%.

CMS said it tweaked the proposed 340B reimbursement cut based on 340B ceiling price data from the Health Resources and Services Administration, with the baseline reductions informed by a drug acquisition cost survey it conducted earlier this year. Those changes will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by $4.35 billion and the drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion (or $900 on average per beneficiary who receives an affected drug from a hospital outpatient department) in the policy’s first year, CMS said.

The rate adjustment did little to calm hospital industry groups who’d railed against the 340B reimbursement changes as a threat to safety-net care and a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate in the subsidy program but would benefit from the budget-neutral offset. The American Hospital Association, the Association of American Medical Colleges and America’s Essential Hospitals each condemned the finalized policy in reaction statements, with the latter two issuing more forceful rebukes.

“CMS has based its reimbursement to 340B hospitals on the results of a hasty and faulty survey, failing to follow the clear requirements of the Medicare statute,” AAMC Chief Health Care Officer Jonathan Jaffery, M.D., said. “The drug payment cuts disproportionately affect and target non-profit and public hospitals serving low-income patients, while redistributing billions of dollars to hospitals that do not share the same safety-net and academic missions. These cuts threaten access to critical services made possible by the 340B program and will lead to worse health outcomes for patients.”

“Rather than strengthening and preserving safety net funding, CMS is instead prioritizing hospitals that do not serve the safety net and nodding to the pharmaceutical industry's interests,” AEH’s statement reads. “These cuts are landing at a time when essential hospitals and their mission are more important than ever, as millions of people risk losing their Medicaid coverage in the coming months.”

The Federation of American Hospitals, which represents for-profit hospitals that do not participate in 340B, struck a different tone, calling the rulemaking “a win for patients, taxpayers and the hospitals that communities depend on.”

“By bringing Medicare drug payments more in line with actual costs, this reform will lower seniors’ out-of-pocket expenses and redirect billions in Medicare dollars where they’re needed most—supporting access to care for patients served by small and rural hospitals across the country,” Charlene MacDonald, the group’s president and CEO, said in a statement. “We applaud the Administration for advancing a smarter, fairer approach to Medicare payment.”

Additionally, CMS finalized an increase in an annual OPPS conversion factor to non-drug items and services, speeding up the agency’s effort to offset a prior $7.8 billion recoupment to 340B hospitals it was forced to make after previously reducing 340B rates contrary to law. But while this accelerated payback—often described by non-340B hospitals as a clawback—was proposed as an increase from 0.5% to 3%, the final rule brings the conversion factor to 2%.

AHA Senior Vice President of Public Policy Analysis and Development Ashley Thompson described both 340B policy changes together as a “continued assault” on the subsidy program that “will further stress hospitals’ ability to care for their patients.” AAMC’s Jaffery said the combined policies’ impact “will be devastating to patients,” and that his group “remains committed to pursuing all available avenues to reverse these payment cuts.”

Further rankling the hospital industry was the final rule’s continued push toward site-neutral payment policy and a phase-out of the inpatient-only list.

For the former, the agency will apply Physician Fee Schedule payment rates for some imaging services to off-campus provider-based departments. In line with the proposed rule, CMS said it expects the plan to trigger first-year reductions in Medicare Part B expenditures and beneficiary cost-sharing obligations of $260 million and $70 million, while also reducing a market incentive for provider consolidation.

Meanwhile, CMS finalized its proposal to remove 647 services from the inpatient-only list, allowing them to be delivered and paid for in the lower-cost outpatient setting.

“Both policies are misguided,” AHA’s Thompson said, “and overlook the unique role hospital outpatient departments play in delivering care to patients in communities nationwide. Hospital outpatient departments treat sicker and more complex groups of patients than independent physician practices, including those with higher rates of disability and who are more likely to come from low-income and rural communities.”

CMS’ fact sheet on the 1,270-page annual rule also noted various changes to quality reporting programs for hospital outpatient departments and ASCs, a proposal to require prior authorization for eight botulinum toxin injection codes CMS said it has seen a jump in claim volume, and new permission for accreditation organizations to assess hospitals’ compliance with EMTALA (the Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act of 1986).

“CMS is committed to spending taxpayer funds wisely and efficiently, so [that] America’s seniors can continue getting the care they need,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a release. “By right-sizing payments and rooting out waste, today’s reforms will drive affordability in Medicare for current beneficiaries while ensuring it will still be there to serve their children and grandchildren.”

#5740. Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age

Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

#5739. Retatrutide Is One Click Away. That Doesn't Make it Safe.

— Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what's in a gray-market vial

A few clicks, a credit card, and a package arrives at your door. The same technology that has expanded access to information and consumer goods has also made it easier than ever for unregulated products to reach consumers while masquerading as legitimate medicine.

As an endocrinologist who treats obesity and diabetes, I have watched new therapies transform care for a complex chronic disease. I also regularly have patients asking about products they found online, on social media, at a medical spa, or through friends and family. Their curiosity and desire for affordable treatment options make sense. But their safety depends on knowing what a product actually is, and whether it has been tested to the standards we expect of any medicine.

Those standards exist for good reason. Before a complex medication reaches patients, it goes through years of laboratory research and progressively larger clinical trials that establish whether it works, for which patients, at what dose, and with what risks. It is then produced by an approved manufacturer under strict quality controls, in facilities subject to inspection, and monitored for safety after it reaches the market. This system allows a physician to safely prescribe a drug for a specific condition, and a patient to trust what is in their syringe.

Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) went through that process and were approved by FDA. But products sold online or at medical spas using the same ingredient names, semaglutide and tirzepatide, do not automatically carry the same safeguards.

Their success has fueled excitement about what comes next.

Retatrutide, often marketed online as "Reta" or "GLP-3," is the latest example. (Side note: the nickname is a misnomer. The molecule acts on three hormone receptors -- GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon -- making it more accurately a "triple-G" agonist.) Results from phase 3 clinical trials in obesity and type 2 diabetes were recently presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes meeting in Milan, with simultaneous publication in the New England Journal of Medicine and The Lancet. The results are impressive, but retatrutide remains investigational and is not approved for any use.

Just as important, the retatrutide studied in those trials is not what is being sold online. Clinical trial participants receive drugs made to exacting specifications, at carefully defined doses and escalation schedules, under close medical monitoring. A gray-market vial labeled "retatrutide" may or may not contain the actual molecule. It may contain more or less than the label claims, or impurities and contaminants no one has tested for. And because there is no established dose for a product of unknown content, buyers are left to mix and inject based on guesswork from online forums. Promising data on the real drug tell us little about what is in that gray-market vial.

The FDA's position is explicit: federal law does not permit retatrutide to be compounded or sold. The agency notes that retatrutide is not an ingredient in any FDA-approved drug and has not been shown to be safe and effective for any condition. Calling a product "compounded retatrutide" does not make it an approved or lawful treatment, and a "for research use only" label does not make it safe. The FDA urges consumers not to buy these products, warning that their quality is unknown and they may harm patients' health.

The agency has also taken enforcement action. In a March 2026 warning letter to Gram Peptides, FDA identified products marketed as retatrutide as unapproved new drugs and said introducing them into interstate commerce violated federal law. It warned that injectables can cause serious harm because they bypass the body's key defenses against toxins and microorganisms. No professional-looking website or glowing testimonial can confirm a product's identity, strength, purity, or sterility.

We, as clinicians, must help patients navigate this landscape without judgment. We need to create a space where patients feel comfortable bringing advertisements and questions into the exam room, where we can review the evidence together and address access issues.

My advice to my patients is clear: do not buy or use retatrutide until it is FDA approved and available from the legitimate manufacturer. In the meantime, I encourage them to ask me or another provider which FDA-approved treatments may fit their needs and how to obtain them through a licensed pharmacy. If investigational treatments interest them, I encourage them to ask about legitimate clinical trials.

Technology can support informed healthcare decisions, but it cannot replace medical guidance. The next step toward better health should begin with a patient-doctor conversation -- not an online checkout.

Cigna offered investors additional color on its new healthcare transformation strategy on Thursday morning.

First unveiled at the company's investor day on Sept. 30, the Lead to One initiative aims to bring together the array of assets under the Cigna Group's umbrella—from medical and pharmacy benefits to behavioral health to specialty care—to address the individual needs of members and patients.

CEO Brian Evanko said during Cigna's earnings call that the program aims to lean on data analytics and technology to identify risks more quickly and deliver personalized supports. The goal, he said, is to drive better outcomes while lowering healthcare costs in tandem.

"Our Lead to One vision will benefit all customers, and we see a particular opportunity with the most clinically complex patient needs, where healthcare costs are increasingly concentrated and represent over 50% of total healthcare spending," he said.

Evanko said that the approach helps to establish "clear strategic growth framework for creating long-term value."

"It is an exciting time here at The Cigna Group as our company unifies around a single vision, Lead to One, and begins to compound the distinctive capabilities we have developed to capture the opportunity set in front of us," he said.

In addition, the company is undertaking an initiative called Accelerate to One, which aims to support operational efficiency for its workforce while supporting greater accountability and better decision-making. Evanko said that program is set to drive $3 billion in run rate savings for the company by 2030.

Evanko said the company expects to see those savings opportunities materialize across the company.

Cigna is the latest health insurance company to boost its guidance for the year on the back of its Q3 results.

The company released its earnings report Thursday morning, posting $1.4 billion in profit. That's down year over year from the $1.9 billion haul the company reported in the third quarter of 2025.

In addition, revenues for the quarter were $73.7 billion, up from $69.7 billion in the prior-year quarter. Both figures surpassed Wall Street analysts' predictions, per Zacks Investment Research.

Through the first three quarters of the year, the company has earned $4.8 billion in profit, on par with the $4.7 billion posted for the first nine months of 2025. Total revenue at the end of Q3 was $213.8 billion, growing from $202.4 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO Brian Evanko said in the release that the company's current financial strategy is rooted in three key principles, including "driving core growth, leveraging our distinct capabilities and executing with discipline."

"As we put our strategy in action, our strong third quarter results demonstrate how we are building on this momentum by making health care more affordable and personalized, while advancing Accelerate to One to drive productivity, reduce costs, and support sustained long-term earnings growth," he said.

The company reported a medical loss ratio in the quarter of 85%, up slightly from 84.8% in Q3 2025. Cigna attributed the uptick to higher costs in its employer plans, while lower costs in the individual market segment did partially offset this trend.

Cigna Healthcare, the company's core insurance business, reported 18.45 million members as of Q3. By comparison, the insurer had 18.1 million members at the end of 2025.

Pharmacy benefit membership, meanwhile, was 117.7 million, down 123.6 million as of Dec. 31, 2025. Cigna said the decrease reflects "expected client transitions" as well as lower membership at its health plan clients.

Its Evernorth unit reported $63.8 billion in adjusted revenue for the quarter, up from $61.5 billion a year ago. Highlights include ongoing organic growth in its specialty pharmacy business, the company said.

Cigna Healthcare reported $11.7 billion in adjusted revenue for Q3, up from $10.7 billion in the prior-year quarter. The company said this largely reflects higher premium revenue as it adapts to higher medical costs.

On the back of the results, Cigna elevated its outlook and now expects at least $30.60 in earnings per share for 2026. It also projects a full-year MLR of 84.2%.

#5736. Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal

Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

#5734. Lp(a)-Lowering Pelacarsen Shows Huge Disconnect With Cardiovascular Outcomes

— After disappointing Lp(a) HORIZON trial, eyes turn to next-gen siRNA therapies

Lowering lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), did not translate into better cardiovascular outcomes in a secondary prevention population, at least not with pelacarsen in the Lp(a) HORIZON trial.

Among people with elevated lipoprotein(a) and pre-existing cardiovascular disease (CVD), pelacarsen was no help for reducing the primary endpoint of cardiovascular death, nonfatal stroke, nonfatal myocardial infarction (MI), or urgent coronary revascularization over nearly 5 years (HR 1.02 compared with placebo, 95% CI 0.90-1.15), reported Steven Nissen, MD, of the Cleveland Clinic, at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting in Chicago.

No matter how the investigators sliced and diced the data, it was the same story: analysis of people with especially high lipoprotein(a), 90 mg/dL or higher, also yielded no benefit (HR 1.00, 95% CI 0.87-1.15); pelacarsen similarly showed no efficacy regarding a modified cardiovascular endpoint not counting revascularizations, another composite endpoint including coronary heart disease rather than cardiovascular deaths, and the individual outcomes of MI, stroke, urgent revascularization, and cardiovascular death.

Beyond these "completely neutral" results, "tolerability issues were certainly very prominent" with pelacarsen, Nissen added during an AHA press conference, citing rates of adverse events leading to drug discontinuation of 20.6% with pelacarsen versus 7.5% with placebo.

Nissen stressed that it may be the end of the road for pelacarsen, but not the lipoprotein(a) hypothesis.

"The Lp(a) HORIZON trial is not the end of the story. Ongoing trials are studying different populations, like primary prevention, aortic stenosis, and different therapies, and siRNA, several siRNAs. A single trial does not provide definitive evidence of a lack of benefit of lowering lipoprotein(a) as a strategy to reduce cardiovascular risk," he said.

Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic CVD and aortic stenosis. It is a highly atherogenic particle considered unmodifiable with diet or physical activity, unlike LDL cholesterol. Estimates suggest one in five people worldwide have high lipoprotein(a).

Pelacarsen was an antisense oligonucleotide made to degrade the hepatic mRNA coding for apolipoprotein(a), an intermediate to the production of lipoprotein(a).

In Lp(a) HORIZON, pelacarsen did drastically reduce lipoprotein(a) and LDL cholesterol by an estimated 77.7% and 13.3%, respectively, relative to placebo. This was on top of existing secondary prevention therapies that had gotten baseline LDL cholesterol to a median 64.6 mg/dL and systolic blood pressure to 125 mmHg on average.

"Was there no room left for improvement? To the credit of the investigators, what was done was actually optimization of what we know to do already: optimize the LDL, optimize the blood pressure. If we do that, was there just no room left in these patients to further reduce the risk?" posed panelist Donald Lloyd-Jones, MD, ScM, of Boston University.

"Like Dr. Nissen, I personally would not recommend that we abandon considering Lp(a) as a potential causal risk factor or as a therapeutic target until we have a lot more data available in different patient populations, certainly in younger individuals and primary prevention populations, over longer periods of time and with ... different chemical strategies to try to inhibit this molecule," said Lloyd-Jones, a past president of the AHA.

Nissen noted that the siRNA therapies in development are potentially more tolerable and more effective while requiring less frequent administration. Already advancing to large-scale cardiovascular outcome trials, for example, are lepodisiran and olpasiran, with others further back in the pipeline.

There's also evidence that the now-familiar PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies reduce Lp(a) along with LDL cholesterol, which may partly explain some of their benefit in CVD risk reduction, according to Lloyd-Jones.

"We don't fully understand the biology here, and I think we need to continue to take a deeper dive into that biology so that we fully understand what it is about Lp(a) that serves as a marker of risk and potentially as a better target for our future therapies," he said.

"I really think you cannot close the door with a single negative trial," Nissen emphasized. "It's going to be my mission to try to convince the people that pay the bills, which is industry sponsors, not to pull the plug on trials because we really need to understand more."

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was a phase III cardiovascular outcomes trial conducted in nearly 800 sites in 42 countries. Eligible participants had a cardiovascular event 3 months to 10 years prior to enrollment and lipoprotein(a) levels 70 mg/dL or greater. They underwent a risk factor optimization period to ensure use of secondary prevention therapies.

Nissen's group had 8,350 individuals randomized 1:1 to pelacarsen 80 mg or placebo self-administered once monthly subcutaneously.

Mean age was just under 60, with about 27% of participants being women and 78% white. Median lipoprotein(a) was 236 nmol/L and hsCRP 0.8 mg/L. Nearly 80% of the cohort were on high-intensity statins.

Follow-up reached a median 57 months in the trial.

Nissen reported that his group sought to conduct additional exploratory analyses on account of the "unexpected" results of Lp(a) HORIZON.

In this extension report, there was still no argument to be made for pelacarsen's efficacy even after accounting for treatment adherence, first and repeated adverse events, and magnitude of 3-month lipoprotein(a) reductions, among other analyses.

Lp(a) HORIZON trial was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine and its extension report separately released in NEJM Evidence.
